title: West, north, below, above
hookLine: spouses, friends, workers, religious teachers: duties both ways
last: RESPECT FLOWS UP, CARE FLOWS DOWN.

lines: EASY TO THANK ONLY ONE OR TWO.
cards: Count the people behind an ordinary day. The person you live with. The friend who texted.

The person who made your coffee, or cleaned the office, or delivered the package. Someone whose words you turn to when life gets heavy. Four kinds of people, and it's easy to thank only one or two of them.
The last part of the Sigalovada finishes the circle: four more directions, four more pairs of duties.

teach.h: WEST: RESPECT, TRUST, A SHARE OF AUTHORITY.
teach.b: West is the spouse. The husband, in the sutta's world, honors his wife by respecting her, by never looking down on her, by being faithful, by giving her authority in the home, and by giving her gifts.
She in return organizes the household well, is kind to both families and to the helpers, is faithful, protects what they've earned, and is skilled and tireless in her work. North is friends.
You honor them by giving, by kind words, by helping, by treating them as equals, and by keeping your word.
They in return look after you when you're careless, guard your things, are a refuge when you're afraid, don't leave you in trouble, and care about your family too. Below are those who work for you.

teach.h: BELOW: FAIR WORK, CARE, TIME OFF.
teach.b: You give them work suited to their strength, food and wages, care when they're sick, a share of special treats, and time off.
They rise before you, rest after you, take only what's given, do good work, and speak well of you. Above are the spiritual teachers, the monks and brahmins of Sigala's day.
You honor them with kindness in deed, word and thought, by keeping your door open to them, and by supplying their needs.
They in return keep you from wrong, encourage what's good, care for you with a kind heart, teach you what you haven't heard, clarify what you have, and show you the way to a heavenly rebirth.
Some details belong to their own century. Care in sickness and days off for workers still read as fresh. Six directions, and in each one, care going both ways.

how: Lay Buddhists learn the Sigalovada's duties as a guide to marriage, friendship and work, and households support monastics with food and requisites while monastics teach and counsel in return.

o: strangers and guests from far away
the dead, toward the setting sun
the spouse, in the six directions

games.q: west, north, below, above: tap the pairs.

s: the Sigalovada gives workers time off
along with fair work, food and wages, care when sick and a share of treats.
in DN 31 only the wife has duties in a marriage
the husband owes five duties too, including respect and faithfulness.
spiritual teachers owe nothing in return for support
they keep you from wrong, encourage good and teach you what you haven't heard.

games.q: you're the head of a household in the Sigalovada. one of your workers falls sick. what does the sutta say you owe?
o: nothing until they come back to work.
games.why: care when sick is one of the five duties toward those who work for you, with fair work, wages, treats and time off.

practice: Turn your attention to someone who works for you or serves you, someone you employ, a cleaner, a driver, the person at the counter, and let one wish for them come up: good health, fair pay, a rest.
Then let the circle widen, west to the person you live with, north to a friend, above to whoever guides you, one face for every direction.

wordCard.voice: West. In DN 31 the west is one's spouse; then north for friends, below for workers, above for spiritual teachers, each with duties both ways. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pacchima disa: the western direction, which DN 31 gives to one's spouse.

carryVoice: Your line: every direction. A bow that began in grief now holds a whole life. That's day five hundred seventy-one.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), the western, northern, lower and upper directions
